article_title: Enhanced Proactive Reading (English Language Learners)
citation: Enhanced Proactive Reading. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Supplemental small-group daily reading instruction pattern for struggling first-grade English learners
description: The intervention pattern evaluated in both trials is daily supplemental reading instruction delivered in small groups of three to five students with homogeneous reading achievement, in a pull-out setting, as an addition to the core reading program. Each 50-minute lesson combines about 40 minutes of lesson delivery with 10 minutes of oracy practice, and activities include word games for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence practice, letter writing, and learning new letter sounds. Instructors "provide opportunities for participation from all students and give feedback for student responses", with largely choral student responses, teacher modeling of new content, and fast-paced lessons monitored for progress.
requirements: Teachers receive 12 hours of professional development before implementation and six additional hours six weeks after the start, plus frequent staff development sessions and on-site coaching
Delivered as a supplement to the regular reading instruction, not a replacement for it
constraints: Evaluated only with first-grade Hispanic English language learners in Texas schools at risk for reading problems
In the Vaughn, Mathes, et al. (2006) trial, comparison students received an average of 63.7 hours of supplemental instruction from other sources, with wide variability
target_learners: First-grade English language learners scoring below the 25th percentile in early reading
target_learning_goals: Early reading skills: phonemic awareness, letter knowledge, word recognition, text fluency, and comprehension strategies
examples: Both reviewed trials implemented the pattern from October to May in four Texas schools each, with fidelity checked via checklists and observations and found acceptable
key_sources: Enhanced Proactive Reading. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Check & Connect
citation: Dropout Prevention intervention report: Check & Connect. (2015). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Sustained monitor-based check-and-connect mentoring pattern
description: The article describes a recurring instructional-design arrangement: a single monitor who functions as the student's mentor and case worker over multiple years. Monitors provide "basic intervention for all students on their caseload, as well as intensive intervention for students as needed" — regular structured discussions about progress plus intensive problem solving, academic support, and family outreach when risk signs increase. The monitor follows students to different schools as needed.
requirements: Monitors record engagement (attendance, academic performance, disciplinary actions) on a daily basis
Monitors had regular interactions with all students on at least a monthly basis in the 1998 study
constraints: In the 1998 study monitors worked 20 hours a week with an average caseload of 25 students
target_learners: secondary students with disabilities at risk of dropout
target_learning_goals: school engagement
school completion
examples: In the 2005 study, monitors attended an initial orientation workshop, weekly or biweekly staff meetings, and submitted attendance printouts with monitoring sheets for verification
key_sources: Dropout Prevention intervention report: Check & Connect. (2015). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/78

article_title: Examining Student and Teacher Math Learning: Lessons from Three Summer Programs
citation: Gregory Chojnacki, Kate Place, Kara Conroy. (2023). Examining Student and Teacher Math Learning: Lessons from Three Summer Programs. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/examining-student-and-teacher-math-learning-lessons-from-three-summer-programs
title: Design summer math programs with attention to teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment
description: The brief reports that "The three summer programs identified lessons on teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment that would improve future implementation." Findings are intended to "inform school districts on the implementation of summer programs" and to "highlight lessons for program providers seeking to refine their programs."
requirements: Program implementers should attend to teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment.
target_learners: grade 6-8 students in summer math programs
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of summer math learning programs
examples: The three evaluated programs generated implementation lessons in teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment for future rounds.

article_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study
citation: Glazerman, S., Isenberg, E., Dolfin, S., Bleeker, M., Johnson, A., Grider, M., & Jacobus, M. (2010). Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Sustain comprehensive induction supports for new teachers across two years to affect student achievement
description: Because the randomized evaluation found achievement impacts only for teachers receiving two years of comprehensive induction and none for one year, induction supports for new teachers should be sustained across two years rather than compressed into a single year. The report states that "two years of comprehensive induction can boost student achievement" while for one year "there was no impact."
requirements: Comprehensive induction components (trained full-time mentors, intensive curriculum, observation opportunities, assessment tools) sustained over two years
constraints: One year of induction showed no impact; no other outcomes were affected
target_learning_goals: Raise student achievement through improved early-career teaching
examples: The evaluation compared teachers receiving one versus two years of comprehensive induction with business-as-usual induction programs
key_sources: Glazerman, S., Isenberg, E., Dolfin, S., Bleeker, M., Johnson, A., Grider, M., & Jacobus, M. (2010). article_title: Suspending Chicago's Students
citation: Sartain, L., Allensworth, E., & Porter, S. (2014). Suspending Chicago's Students: Differences in Discipline across Schools. UChicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide supportive school climates for students facing concentrated disadvantage, since suspensions cost instructional time and worsen falling behind
description: The report's authors argue that students with the most disadvantages most need a supportive school climate and too often do not get one. As co-author Elaine Allensworth states, such students are "more likely to be suspended, miss even more instructional time, and fall further behind". The principle directs schools serving high-poverty, low-achievement populations toward climate supports and alternatives to suspension, informed by the report's findings that suspensions concentrate in disadvantaged schools and associate with worse climate.
requirements: Schools must be able to implement alternative discipline approaches such as restorative justice rather than relying on suspensions
constraints: The report found policy solutions are particularly difficult to implement effectively in schools with the most disciplinary problems
target_learners: Students in high-poverty, low-achievement urban schools
African-American boys at racially diverse schools
target_learning_goals: Reducing lost instructional time
Improving school climate and peer relationships
examples: The report found almost a third of students with a history of abuse or neglect were suspended in 2013-14, and shortening suspensions was associated with improved attendance but worse climate
key_sources: Sartain, L., Allensworth, E., & Porter, S. (2014). Suspending Chicago's Students: Differences in Discipline across Schools. UChicago Consortium. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/suspending-chicagos-students-differences-discipline-practices-across-schools

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use multi-measure school survey reports to support self-assessment and improvement planning
description: The report is designed to supplement test-score data in school improvement planning: it is "intended to supplement your assessments of test-score data and other performance indicators on the School Improvement Plan for Advancing Academic Achievement." By identifying areas that are strong, weak, strengthening, or weakening over time, the profiles can stimulate discussion among the principal, teachers, and Local School Council about priorities, partnerships, community resources, and student safety.
requirements: Survey participation meeting response-rate thresholds so measures can be validly computed
constraints: Measure definitions indicate whether items are positive or negative measures; on Incidence of Disciplinary Action, low scores are desirable
target_learners: principals, teachers, Local School Council members, and school improvement teams
target_learning_goals: setting improvement priorities and planning school development
examples: The report provides guiding questions under each profile, such as whether school improvement efforts over the last two years reflect a coordinated plan
key_sources: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Jennings, S., & Dean, M. (2003). Torvalds Improving Chicago's Schools: 2003 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-torvalds

article_title: Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education
citation: Angela Johnson, Elizabeth Barker. (2021). Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Provide support during school years so students with disabilities can grow as much as or more than peers
description: The brief's research finds that "with support, students with disabilities grow as much or more academically during the school year than their peers without disabilities during some years." This principle holds that adequate school-year support is the condition under which students with disabilities keep pace academically, and that summer loss, not school-year learning capacity, drives widening gaps.
requirements: School-year support for students with disabilities must be in place for growth to match or exceed peers
constraints: The finding applies to grades K-4 and only some school years, per the brief's description
target_learners: Students with disabilities in grades K-4
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement and growth in reading and mathematics
examples: The brief examined academic achievement and growth of students with and without disabilities in grades K-4, comparing school-year and summer growth patterns
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Elizabeth Barker. (2021). Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/understanding-differential-growth-during-school-years-and-summers-for-students-in-special-education/

article_title: Principal Leadership in a Virtual Environment
citation: Stephenson, S. P., Hardy, A., Seylar, J., Wayman, J., Peters, V., Bellin, M., & Roschelle, J. (2021). Equity-Centered Leadership in a Virtual Environment. The Wallace Foundation. https://www.wallacefoundation.org
title: Support principals for innovation and risk-taking, including collegial support forms, to build a school culture for technology use
description: To create a school culture for technology use, the report recommends that principals receive "support for innovation and risk-taking, as well as their continuous improvement efforts." Supports may include principal professional learning communities or other social forms of collegial support specifically addressing the challenges of leading in a virtual environment, and the support system should account for how principal needs, preferences, schools, and populations differ.
requirements: Support systems must take account of how principal needs and preferences vary and how schools and populations differ
constraints: The report bases this recommendation on its literature review and interviews with leaders from five recognized districts
target_learning_goals: leading virtual learning environments and fostering school culture for technology use
examples: Domain 5 strategies suggest supplementing one-on-one supervisor support with virtual professional learning communities or communities of practice
key_sources: Stephenson, S. P., Hardy, A., Seylar, J., Wayman, J., Peters, V., Bellin, M., & Roschelle, J. (2021). Equity-Centered Leadership in a Virtual Environment. The Wallace Foundation. https://www.wallacefoundation.org

article_title: Continuing the educator micro-credential movement
citation: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Successful micro-credential implementations share careful messaging, broad buy-in, and educator-led learning systems
description: The report states that "the most successful micro-credential implementations to date are marked by a few key characteristics, including careful messaging around the purpose and value of micro-credentials and the buy-in across a school or district, from classroom educators to administrators." Districts, states, and unions are urged to "build a system of educator-led learning — virtual and face-to-face — that guides how micro-credentials are earned," with new roles for professional development providers, district managers, and university faculty. The report calls clear communication of goals from the start, plus supports throughout, the most important condition for success.
requirements: Communicating clearly about the goals of a micro-credential effort from the get-go and providing the right supports throughout the process
target_learners: K-12 educators, administrators, and district and state professional learning leaders
target_learning_goals: Earning micro-credentials as competency-based professional learning and leadership development
examples: Baltimore County educators worked with school-based instructional coaches on micro-credentials aligned with district priorities; Charlottesville structured its pilot for novice educators and mentors through its Learning Management System
key_sources: Center for Teaching Quality (CTQ) and Digital Promise. (2017). Continuing the educator micro-credential movement. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices
citation: Viki M. Young, Ph.D. and Alexandra Merritt Johnson, Ph.D. (2024). Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Plan for sustainability during the pilot's final phase, covering buy-in, stewardship, budgeting, and data collection
description: The article frames sustainability as a phase following implementation in which teams, with facilitators, plan explicitly for continuation. Teams "engaged in a sustainability planning process with Digital Promise facilitators" whose key topics included buy-in, community-level conditions for scale, ownership and ongoing stewardship, budgeting for ongoing costs, and data collection to evaluate the solution. Planning also sets expectations that the school or community will persist with the solution amid turnover and reform fads.
requirements: Anticipate declining or repurposed resources and address incentives, logistical barriers, and additional resource needs identified during initial implementation
constraints: Because pilots ended between December 2022 and March 2023, sustainability blurred with ongoing implementation through June 2023, and no additional data collection occurred in the 2023-24 school year
target_learners: District-community teams including students, families, teachers, and leaders
target_learning_goals: Sustaining community-developed education solutions and inclusive R&D processes
examples: Teams used meeting notes and sustainability planning templates in the last pilot phase to identify local action steps for sustaining their work
key_sources: Viki M. Young, Ph.D. and Alexandra Merritt Johnson, Ph.D. (2024). Sustainability in Inclusive Innovation: District-Community Solutions, Mindsets, and Practices. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/94695da1-ad96-49e5-b461-b759d617ae25

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Support transformative learning through trust, triggering events, reflection, and action
description: The report recommends that educators "create an environment in which students open their minds to new possibilities about their lives and futures." The sequence is to build trust, facilitate a triggering event that surfaces alternative viewpoints, have learners reflect on those viewpoints, and take some kind of action that crystallizes the transformation.
requirements: Create trust first — comfortable students "will be more likely to share their thoughts, ask questions, and be open to probing or opposing views."
constraints: "Not all students will have a transformative learning experience"; the report frames this type of learning as mattering for some adult learners rather than as a universal outcome.
target_learners: adult learners in online or blended programs
target_learning_goals: motivation and confidence
openness to new perspectives and career possibilities
examples: Suggested trigger activities include reading news articles, simulations, team projects, research, and discussing videos; action steps include publishing a paper, producing a video or photo essay, or researching a new career.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making
citation: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides/
title: Provide supports that foster a data-driven culture: facilitator, structured time, professional development
description: Schools and districts should prepare educators to use data effectively by emphasizing collaborative data use. Checklist actions are designating "a school-based facilitator who meets with teacher teams to discuss data", dedicating structured time for staff collaboration, and providing targeted professional development regularly. Collaboration efforts can create or strengthen shared expectations and common practices regarding data use throughout a school.
requirements: A designated school-based data facilitator
Dedicated structured time for staff collaboration
Regular targeted professional development
target_learning_goals: Collaborative interpretation of student achievement data
examples: Table 3 of the guide lists suggested professional development and training opportunities

article_title: Participation in Math Corps Increases College Enrollment
citation: Barbara Harris, Lindsay Fox. (2022). Participation in Math Corps Increases College Enrollment. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/participation-in-math-corps-increases-college-enrollment
title: Pairing intensive math instruction with emotional and social support in a summer program
description: Math Corps pairs an academic component with a relational one: its founders' "primary goal for the camp was to support the emotional and social needs of the students in Detroit," and they used their math-teaching backgrounds to add "high-quality math instruction" to that support. The pattern is an intensive summer camp format in which mentoring and positive influences are delivered alongside substantive instruction in a school subject, rather than as separate programming.
requirements: Staff with subject-matter teaching backgrounds who can deliver high-quality instruction while also attending to students' emotional and social needs.
constraints: The article describes this pattern as implemented in a summer camp for middle school students in a single city; it does not claim the pattern generalizes to other settings or grade levels.
target_learners: middle school students who could benefit from mentoring and positive influences
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
social and emotional development
examples: Math Corps educators leveraged their backgrounds as math teachers to create an intensive summer program providing both emotional and social support and high-quality math instruction.
key_sources: Barbara Harris, Lindsay Fox. (2022). Participation in Math Corps Increases College Enrollment. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/participation-in-math-corps-increases-college-enrollment

article_title: Summer Bridge Programs
citation: Summer Bridge Programs. (2016). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Supporting Postsecondary Success. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Summer bridge programs combine orientation, advising, college-success skills training, and accelerated coursework in the 2–4 week bridge period
description: Summer bridge programs occur in the summer period between high school and college and, although content varies across institutions and populations, share a characteristic multi-component design. The report states they "typically last 2–4 weeks and involve (a) an in-depth orientation to college life and resources, (b) academic advising, (c) training in skills necessary for college success (e.g., time management and study skills), and/or (d) accelerated academic coursework." Nonacademic components are designed to provide cultural and social capital and promote adjustment to college culture.
requirements: Programs must be delivered in the summer bridge period between high school and college
constraints: Content varies across institutions and by the population served; components are combined with 'and/or', so not all programs include all four
target_learners: Incoming college freshmen, historically targeting ethnic/racial minority, low-income, first-generation, or other at-risk populations
target_learning_goals: College readiness, adjustment to college culture, time management and study skills, academic preparation for college-level work
examples: The Challenge Program implemented this design with non-credit-bearing college-like courses, peer educators and coaches, and family integration activities
key_sources: Summer Bridge Programs. (2016). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Supporting Postsecondary Success. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/661

article_title: The Challenges Facing CPS Administrators
citation: Bruzgulis, A., Hart, H., & Young, C. (2019). The challenges facing CPS administrators: Roadblocks to school improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Policymakers and district staff should target supports at administrators facing substantial roadblocks in nearly every category, especially the one-third reporting considerable roadblocks
description: The brief's interpretive summary recommends that "policymakers and district staff may want to consider which supports can best address administrators' and schools' needs," with the most pressing group being the one-third of administrators reporting substantial roadblocks in nearly every survey category. It frames this as an opportunity for researchers, policymakers, and the district to work together to provide supports that empower administrators, their schools, and their students.
requirements: District-level survey data identifying which administrators face considerable roadblocks, such as the latent class analysis used in this brief
constraints: The brief does not argue for particular policies or programs; it identifies areas that may most benefit from additional support without specifying solutions
target_learners: CPS principals, assistant principals, and other lead administrators
target_learning_goals: School improvement leadership and administrator retention and effectiveness
examples: The brief reports school leaders planned to stay an additional six years on average in their leadership roles regardless of roadblock group, demonstrating willingness to stay engaged and look for solutions
key_sources: Bruzgulis, A., Hart, H., & Young, C. (2019). The challenges facing CPS administrators: Roadblocks to school improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/challenges-facing-cps-administrators

article_title: The Network for College Success
citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: Embed educator learning in sustained professional learning communities rather than one-time professional development
description: The NCS model holds that school improvement requires embedding adult learning in sustained professional learning communities working toward long-term goals. The paper states that "one-time, 'drive-by' professional development is insufficient in creating deep and lasting change." NCS operationalizes this through long-term partnerships and monthly Collaboratives in which school leaders examine research, interrogate data, and share practice in a safe, normed environment. Cross-school sharing of data and practice is built into every session so educators learn from peers facing similar challenges.
requirements: Networks need strong cultures with trusting relationships, norms, and protocols that create a safe space for honest, open problem-solving
constraints: If people perceive that speaking honestly will have negative consequences, the flow of information about problems will be suppressed, making improvement unlikely
target_learners: High school principals, assistant principals, counselors, teacher leaders, and data strategists
target_learning_goals: Leaders' capacity to lead and manage school change and improve student outcomes through collaborative problem-solving
examples: The Principals' Collaborative met monthly in each other's schools to examine problems of practice; practitioners reported that cross-school data sharing pushed them to question their own practices
key_sources: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/network-college-success-capacity-building-model-school-improvement

article_title: Navigating a Sea of Reforms: Sustaining School Health Centers through Statewide Initiatives
citation: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://WestEd.org
title: Sustain school health centers with continued county operational funding alongside new billing initiatives
description: The report concludes that new billing revenues cannot by themselves sustain school health centers: "New funding through the CYBHI's Fee Schedule and CalAIM's ECM benefit do not offer an obvious pathway to replace the county's investment in SHCs with operational funds." County operational funds play a critical role in sustaining SHC staffing models, and most county-funded personnel have little or no billing pathway. The report recommends that Healthy Schools and Communities identify other sustainability strategies, new partners, or expanded county funds to maintain operations.
requirements: Continued county operational grants or alternative sustainability strategies and new partners to maintain current SHC capacity
constraints: Lead agencies face workforce shortages and are navigating multiple reforms simultaneously; SHCs cannot adopt state initiatives without support and buy-in from lead agency decision-makers
target_learners: Children and youth served by Alameda County school health centers
target_learning_goals: Sustained access to school-based health and behavioral health services supporting student well-being and attendance
examples: WestEd analyzed 2024–25 projected budgets for each lead agency and estimated Fee Schedule revenue for five SHCs to assess whether state initiatives could replace county funds
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Sabalburo, E., & Ford, J. (2025). Navigating a sea of reforms: Sustaining school health centers through statewide initiatives. Alameda County Health, Healthy Schools and Communities. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673564

article_title: Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education with Families and Communities
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Codesigning Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education With Families and Communities. WestEd brief. https://education.uw.edu/sites/default/files/programs/epsc/Users%20Guide%20Road%20Map%20Survey.pdf
title: Support mathematics teachers in designing project-based learning opportunities centered on local community needs
description: The brief recommends that school leaders build relationships with local organizations and community leaders well respected by both students and their families, because partnering with such groups "can help level power dynamics and create pathways for teachers to design meaningful project-based learning opportunities" (citing Caires-Hurley et al., 2020). Leaders should provide access to curriculum and training so mathematical tasks can address local community needs.
requirements: Leaders should provide access to curriculum and training to support project-based learning
target_learning_goals: Solidifying mathematical concepts through community-centered project-based learning
examples: Cited examples include public art installations, conservation projects, and urban planning simulations designed to solidify mathematical concepts

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Build intentional support infrastructure for dual enrollment rather than restricting access as a protective strategy
description: Because achievement-based eligibility thresholds screen out capable students while leaving underlying barriers intact, the brief recommends investing in deliberate student supports instead of tightening readiness criteria. It states that "Scaffolding coursework, responding quickly when students are struggling, and providing structured academic support—rather than imposing enrollment screens—are the practices that improve outcomes," and that "Support infrastructure should be treated as a core program cost, not an optional enhancement added after enrollment decisions are made."
requirements: Districts must fund support infrastructure as a core program cost and prepare faculty and staff for college-concurrent environments
constraints: Applies where dual enrollment is designed as an on-ramp for students who would not otherwise access advanced coursework; the brief notes findings may feel like edge cases where it functions mainly as acceleration
target_learners: High school students in or considering dual enrollment, particularly students from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: College enrollment, dual enrollment course success, and equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: The brief recommends districts audit dual enrollment pass rates disaggregated by student subgroup to determine whether outcomes reflect preparation gaps or support gaps
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681344

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Suggested Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 HLS question sets
description: The paper presents candidate HLS questions organized by tier: Tier 1 questions on the student's current receptive and productive language use and exposure across home, school, and outside-of-school contexts; Tier 2 questions on English variety names, adult home language, first language spoken, literacy in English and other languages, and years in U.S. schools; Tier 3 questions on parents' preferred languages for written and oral school communication. The paper cautions that "None of these questions has been piloted for ease of comprehension; they are only suggested starting points."
requirements: Questions should be piloted with parents/guardians and school personnel across a wide range of language groups, in both print and oral forms, and in translation and interpreter formats
constraints: The questions are untested starting points requiring refinement based on focus groups and piloting
target_learners: Parents/guardians of K-12 students at initial school enrollment
target_learning_goals: Identifying students who should proceed to English language proficiency screening
examples: Tier 1 sample question: Which language does your child most often use at home, in school/educational settings, and outside of school
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Sustaining implementation through people, policies, processes, and practices
description: Domain 4 represents the overall goal of leaders' work: sustainable implementation of the NGSS. Leaders continuously assess whether effective implementation has been achieved and what is needed next, examining their impact on four key areas: People, Policies, Processes, and Practices. The article states "leaders examine their impact on four key areas that influence sustaining the use of the NGSS." title: Subject-level demographic MAE-gap fairness regularization for multimodal attention models
description: An in-processing fairness framework that adds a demographic disparity penalty to the training objective of a multimodal attention model. constraints: In this study the validation-level fairness improvements did not consistently generalize to held-out subjects or repeated subject-level splits

target_learning_goals: reducing demographic error disparities in continuous student attention estimation while preserving predictive performance

title: Evaluate fairness-aware learning models with subgroup-aware metrics, repeated subject-level validation, and joint interpretation of disparity and accuracy
description: Because aggregate predictive metrics can conceal demographic disparities and single-split validation can overstate fairness gains, this principle holds that fairness claims require subgroup-level evaluation alongside overall and worst-group error, tested across repeated subject-level splits. The article concludes that "stable fairness improvements require stronger evidence than a single validation split or a reduction in one disparity metric." Disparity metrics should be interpreted jointly with predictive accuracy, since lower disparities do not necessarily correspond to better outcomes for all demographic groups.

Repeated subject-level train-validation-test splits with paired comparisons
Sufficient numbers of independent subjects per subgroup
constraints: With very few subjects per subgroup, subgroup and worst-group metrics can be strongly influenced by individual participant behavior
Automatically inferred rather than self-reported demographic attributes add uncertainty
target_learners: students in demographic subgroups of educational AI deployments
target_learning_goals: reliable, fairness-aware evaluation of automated student attention and engagement estimation
examples: The study evaluated overall MAE, worst-group MAE, and best-to-worst subgroup MAE gaps for each fairness axis, and ran repeated subject-level split experiments with paired baseline and fairness-model comparisons

citation: Nikolai Maurer, Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen, Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Johannes Huwer. (2026). Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs. Computers and Education Open 10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100376
title: AI-related post-qualification for in-service science educators should emphasize school- and subject-specific AI literacy and concrete subject-specific use cases
description: Because general AI literacy did not relate to AI use and use concentrated in general rather than subject-specific DiKoLAN areas, the article concludes that post-qualification courses "should focus on promoting school- and subject-specific AI literacy and highlighting concrete subject-specific usage opportunities". Programs should be designed as an integrated component of the school context and the respective subject, not as a stand-alone offer.
requirements: Programs should build on teachers' existing competencies (PK, PCK, CK) rather than treating them as novices
Access to AI tools must be provided by responsible departments so teachers can take first steps
constraints: The proposed pathways and the role of subject-specific AI literacy in teachers' AI use still require testing in further research
target_learners: in-service secondary science educators in Germany and Switzerland
target_learning_goals: subject-specific AI competencies (TCKAI, TPACKAI)
identifying subject-specific opportunities to use AI in science teaching
examples: Interviewed teachers most often called for subject-specific examples of AI application (n = 11) as professional-development content
The article contrasts the rarely used subject-specific DiKoLAN areas with the DiKoLANAI framework to identify which competencies post-qualification should address
key_sources: Nikolai Maurer, Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen, Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Johannes Huwer. (2026). Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs. Computers and Education Open 10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100376

article_title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Green Education: Optimizing Teacher Workflow and Enhancing Pedagogical Design under Sustainable Development Pedagogy (SDP) Constraints
citation: Hossein Talebzadeh. (2025). The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Green Education: Optimizing Teacher Workflow and Enhancing Pedagogical Design under Sustainable Development Pedagogy (SDP) Constraints. 3rd National Conference on Green Industries Innovation, University of Mazandaran. https://conf.umz.ac.ir/gii
title: Sustainable Development Pedagogy (SDP) AI model converting zero-paper mandates into design catalysts
description: The SDP model (Talebzadeh, 2025b) is an operational constraint framework that integrates "mandatory paperless protocols and fully digitalized assessment workflows" directly into the IAT model. It treats administrative and environmental constraints not as barriers but as primary catalysts for pedagogical innovation, addressing what the article calls "The Green Gap". In the study, teams were mandated to re-engineer their instructional designs under full SDP constraints after green-management prompt training.
requirements: Integration into the IAT model and AI-assisted workflows
constraints: Studied as a constraint imposed on pre-service teachers' instructional design, not on in-service practice
target_learning_goals: resource-efficient, paperless instructional design and assessment workflows
examples: Teams underwent intensive training on SDP prompts (green management protocols) and re-engineered their lesson plans two weeks after the baseline phase

citation: Hossein Talebzadeh. (2025). title: Treat sustainability constraints as catalysts for pedagogical innovation rather than barriers
description: The article argues that rigid environmental and administrative constraints, when coupled with structured AI partnership frameworks, can shift "from being systemic hindrances into potent accelerators for pedagogical innovation". Rather than trading pedagogical quality for compliance, educators should embed zero-paper mandates directly into the design workflow so that efficiency requirements force deeper reflection and workflow redesign. The study's design-leap results are offered as quantitative support for this stance.
requirements: A structured AI partnership framework (the IAT model) mediating the constraint
Training on constraint-aligned prompts
constraints: Evidence comes from a single quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with 28 teams of pre-service geography teachers
target_learning_goals: instructional design quality under sustainability and efficiency constraints
examples: Teams re-engineered lesson plans under a mandated zero-paper constraint after SDP prompt training, with all four rubric indices improving significantly

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Subordinate AI and digitalization to coherent normative, ethical, and governance frameworks that prioritize educational purpose, social justice, and human dignity
description: The article's central design recommendation is that achieving sustainable education in the digital age depends not on AI adoption per se but on governance. It concludes that sustainable education depends "on subordinating AI and digitalization to coherent normative, ethical, and governance frameworks that prioritize educational purpose, social justice, and human dignity". In practice this means embedding equity-oriented design principles, transparent data governance, accountability mechanisms for algorithmic decision-making, and explicit norms of academic integrity in educational policy, so that platform logic is subordinated to educational ethics rather than the reverse.
requirements: Institutions must adopt public-oriented governance frameworks, including transparent data governance, limits on extractive data practices, and accountability mechanisms for algorithmic decision-making
constraints: Positive AI outcomes are contingent upon adequate infrastructure, institutional capacity, teacher training, and pedagogical integration; AI may exacerbate inequality unless equity-oriented governance is deliberately embedded
target_learners: all learners in AI-mediated educational systems, particularly those from low-income, rural, or marginalized backgrounds
target_learning_goals: protecting educational purpose, social justice, human dignity, epistemic integrity, and academic integrity in AI-mediated education
examples: The article's integrated result specifies five conditions for sustainable AI adoption, including public-oriented data governance, deliberative oversight, equity-oriented design, and clear norms of academic integrity and human-centered assessment
key_sources: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257

article_title: The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1
title: Successive relearning: a technique combining spacing and retrieval practice
description: Successive relearning is a learning technique that combines spacing and retrieval practice, presented in the review as a potent method for obtaining and maintaining knowledge. The review devotes figures to the "Successive relearning paradigm" and "Successive relearning results", and cites work describing it as "an effective learning technique that combines spacing and retrieval". It is illustrated with classic evidence of spaced retrieval practice benefiting foreign language vocabulary retention in adults over years.
requirements: Requires repeated retrieval practice episodes distributed over time (spaced) rather than massed
target_learners: students in courses with durable retention goals
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of knowledge such as foreign language vocabulary
examples: The review cites a classic study demonstrating benefits of spaced retrieval practice (successive relearning) on foreign language vocabulary in adults over a period of 5 years
key_sources: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1

article_title: How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works – A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Renkl, A., Atkinson, R.K. & Große, C.S. (2004). How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works – A Cognitive Load Perspective. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:TRUC.0000021815.74806.f6
title: Fade out worked solution steps successively to support the transition from example study to problem solving
description: This principle holds that, to move learners from studying worked examples in early skill acquisition to independent problem solving, instruction should "successivelyfade out worked solution steps" rather than using traditional example-problem pairs. The article examines this from a cognitive load perspective across two computer-based experiments. The mechanism the authors ultimately identify is reduced unproductive learning events rather than increased self-explanations.
requirements: A computer-based or otherwise structured learning environment in which worked solution steps can be successively faded across the progression from examples to problems
constraints: The position of the faded steps did not influence learning outcomes, so the principle does not specify a particular fading position; the hypothesized self-explanation trigger mechanism was not confirmed in the think-aloud analysis
target_learners: Learners in earlier stages of skill acquisition transitioning to problem solving
target_learning_goals: Cognitive skill acquisition and problem solving
examples: Two experiments used a computer-based learning environment containing faded worked solution steps; Experiment 2 collected thinking-aloud protocols during learner interaction with the environment.
key_sources: Renkl, A., Atkinson, R.K. & Große, C.S. (2004). How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works – A Cognitive Load Perspective. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:TRUC.0000021815.74806.f6

article_title: Shared Picture Book Reading Interventions for Child Language Development: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dowdall, N., Melendez-Torres, G. J., Murray, L., Gardiner, F., Harrtford, L. & Cooper, P.J. (2020). Shared picture book reading interventions for child language development: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development, 91(2). https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13225
title: Deliver book-sharing interventions with sufficient dosage (multiple sessions, over 60 minutes of contact time)
description: The review concludes that brief interventions are unlikely to improve children's language, while multi-session programmes with extended instructor-caregiver contact time are highly likely to do so. It states that "brief interventions being unlikely to result in improvements in children's language abilities" whereas "Interventions involving multiple sessions, on the other hand, with extended contact time between the instructor and caregiver, are highly likely to result in improvements to child language." The principle is to design caregiver training with enough sessions and contact time to change caregiver book-sharing behaviour.
requirements: Training must exceed roughly 60 minutes of collective contact time, delivered across multiple sessions with an instructor
constraints: The dose categorization was crude (a near median split at 60 minutes); the dose contrast for expressive language showed only weak evidence (p=0.07) and for receptive language was non-significant (p=0.11)
target_learning_goals: Child expressive and receptive language development through interactive shared picture book reading
examples: In the included studies, dose varied from a nurse spending approximately five minutes during well-child visits discussing shared reading to an 18-session home programme; 10 of the 19 studies involved training time in excess of 60 minutes with caregivers
key_sources: Dowdall, N., Melendez-Torres, G. J., Murray, L., Gardiner, F., Harrtford, L. & Cooper, P.J. (2020). Shared picture book reading interventions for child language development: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development, 91(2). https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13225

article_title: BICS-CALP: An Introduction for Some, a Review for Others
citation: Roessingh, H. (2006). BICS-CALP: An Introduction for Some, a Review for Others. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 23(2), Spring 2006. https://www.tesl.ca
title: Provide sustained ESL support across the school years because academic language development outlasts the two-year BICS period
description: The principle holds that ESL learners need language support well beyond the point at which conversational fluency appears, because the below-the-surface CALP mass takes far longer to develop. The author argues that "after BICS-level language has been acquired, the distances to the next benchmark or threshold become greater and more difficult to reach," and that quality and duration of ESL programming are crucial. She recommends continued support even for proficient older arrivals as they outgrow their L1.
requirements: Quality and duration of ESL programming, which the author calls crucial
Direct vocabulary instruction in context, which the author calls equally important and crucial for the ESL learner
constraints: The author notes policymakers who would like to limit funding for ESL programs seek shortcuts, which she argues against
target_learners: ESL learners of all ages in K-12 and postsecondary settings
target_learning_goals: Reaching the academic language proficiency threshold required for postsecondary study
examples: The author reports that 750 contact hours of high school ESL support can have a tangible effect toward the postsecondary threshold

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Success criteria and learning intentions as components of formative practice.
description: In a note, the article identifies explicitly communicated goals for learning as an important component of formative classroom practice: "The importance of “success criteria” and “learning intentions” was emphasised by Clarke (2001)." Success criteria and learning intentions function as elements that make the intended learning visible to students, supporting the regulation of learning that the article's framework treats as central to formative assessment. The article cites this emphasis rather than developing it at length in the accessible text.
requirements: Teachers must articulate learning intentions and success criteria so that students know what valued learning looks like.
constraints: The article attributes the emphasis to Clarke (2001) and does not elaborate implementation detail in the accessible text.
target_learners: School students whose teachers share learning intentions and success criteria
target_learning_goals: Clarifying intended learning and criteria for success to support self-regulation
examples: The article's note cites Clarke (2001) as the source emphasising success criteria and learning intentions.
key_sources: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: Sustain strategy instruction over multiple years, gradually shifting regulation from teacher to student
description: The article argues that "it takes time to become a strategic self-regulated reader" and that "strategy instruction should be sustained and should gradually shift from external regulation by the teacher to internal regulation by the students." Accordingly, SRI was implemented over two school years: in Grade 3 the teacher modeled all strategies, while in Grade 4 students were frequently asked to assist in modeling, and the visualizing strategy shifted from mental imagery to creating graphic representations of text.
requirements: A two-year implementation window in Grades 3 and 4 with repeated teacher training each year
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated reading strategy use
Independent strategic reading
examples: In Grade 4, when preparing a summary, the teacher and students together determined which information was more important

article_title: The influence of concept mapping on achievement, self-regulation, and self-efficacy in students of English as a second language
citation: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889
title: Survey of Learning Behaviors as the measure of self-regulation strategies
description: The Survey of Learning Behaviors is one of the study's instruments, listed in the Method chapter alongside the achievement test. It was used to measure students' self-regulation, which in this study "involves the students' self-monitoring and knowledge acquisition strategies," showing "the extent to which students can use the strategies for studying, how well they can understand the concepts they are studying, and how often they will check and correct their understanding of these concepts." It was administered at pretest and posttest to both treatment groups.
requirements: Administered as a pretest and posttest measure alongside the other dependent variables.
target_learning_goals: Measuring self-monitoring and knowledge acquisition strategy use
examples: The instrument appears as Appendix B of the dissertation.

article_title: Visual attention, behavioral inhibition and speech/language outcomes in deaf children with cochlear implants
citation: Horn, D. L., Davis, R. A. O., Pisoni, D. B., & Miyamoto, R. T. (2004). Visual attention, behavioral inhibition and speech/language outcomes in deaf children with cochlear implants. Int Congr Ser. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ics.2004.07.048
title: Subvocal rehearsal and executive function account for the dCPT–outcome relation in deaf children with cochlear implants
description: The article proposes that the dCPT delay task taps cognitive skills tied to speech and language outcomes, offering two candidate mechanisms. It states that "Performance on the dCPT might be more influenced by subvocal rehearsal strategies which are related to speech perception, production, and language measures in deaf children with CIs," citing prior working-memory work, or alternatively that the dCPT loads more heavily on executive functions including behavioral analysis and synthesis. The framework explains why the dCPT, but not the vCPT, correlated with outcomes.
requirements: Further research is needed, as the article states more research is needed to understand how these functions play a role in deaf children acquiring speech-language skills with a CI
constraints: The account is offered as interpretation, not tested within this study
target_learners: prelingually deaf children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: spoken language development
speech perception and production
executive function and behavioral inhibition
examples: The dCPT required children to figure out a delay rule of at least 4 s between button presses from visual score-counter feedback in 6 min, which the authors suggest loads on rehearsal or executive control
key_sources: Horn, D. L., Davis, R. A. O., Pisoni, D. B., & Miyamoto, R. T. (2004). Visual attention, behavioral inhibition and speech/language outcomes in deaf children with cochlear implants. Int Congr Ser. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ics.2004.07.048

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Supervised versus unsupervised machine learning methods for automating analysis of learning data
description: The article introduces the machine learning distinction it uses to organize the special issue. "In supervised methods, we begin with a set of instances of data that have already been labeled (i.e., coded), usually by a human coder," producing a classifier that labels uncoded items, with data divided into training, testing, and optionally held-out corpora. "In contrast, unsupervised methods seek to discover structure in data that have not previously been labeled," typically via clustering that requires defining a similarity measure. Unsupervised methods add the burden of interpreting whether clusters are meaningful.
requirements: Supervised classification requires the analyst to determine which features of items are most helpful for predicting labels; unsupervised clustering requires defining a measure of similarity between pairs of data items.
constraints: The article warns that unsupervised clusters "might not turn out to be particularly meaningful" and, if meaningful, may not match categories useful for the research.
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers applying computational methods to learning data
target_learning_goals: Understanding when to use labeled-classification versus structure-discovery approaches for learning data
examples: Two special issue articles (Gobert et al.; Baker et al.) use supervised classification; three (Berland et al.; Sherin; Blikstein et al.) use unsupervised methods.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood
citation: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x
title: Foster supportive school environments and close interpersonal connections to support intrinsic motivation among ethnic-minority students facing stigma
description: The article suggests that supportive school environments may be important sources of intrinsic motivation among some ethnic-minority children in the face of stigma. School belonging—students' emotional connection with their school and the people at their school—was associated with higher intrinsic motivation and mediated the higher intrinsic motivation of Dominican children. The authors state that interventions aimed at helping students from Latin-American backgrounds maintain academic motivation may benefit from fostering close interpersonal connections at school.
requirements: School belonging must be measured or cultivated as students' emotional connection with their school and the people at their school
constraints: The mediational findings do not imply causality
The Dominican finding may have been due to school-specific factors, as almost all Dominican participants were drawn from two schools
target_learners: elementary-age children from ethnic-minority and immigrant backgrounds
target_learning_goals: maintaining intrinsic motivation for school in the face of stigmatization
examples: For Dominican students, school belonging partially compensated for stigma by contributing directly to higher intrinsic motivation, despite lower public regard
key_sources: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x

article_title: Relative Effectiveness of Reading Intervention Programs for Adults With Low Literacy
citation: Sabatini John P., Shore Jane, Holtzman Steven, Scarborough Hollis S. (2011). Relative Effectiveness of Reading Intervention Programs for Adults with Low Literacy. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3269067/
title: Supplemental one-on-one tutoring in decoding and fluency can improve basic reading skills of low-literate adults beyond routine classroom instruction
description: The article argues that adult literacy classrooms rarely target decoding, word recognition, or fluency systematically, and that supplemental one-on-one tutoring adapted from child-focused programs can address these gaps. The authors state that "it is reasonable to attribute any observed gains largely to the supplemental tutoring that directly and intensively addressed the participants' deficiencies in decoding and fluency." The principle holds that adults with basic reading skills below seventh grade level benefit from explicit, structured tutoring in foundational skills.
requirements: Tutors trained in a structured program with fidelity monitoring
Sessions delivered about three times per week over roughly 10-18 weeks
Participants screened for limited word recognition skills
constraints: No control group, so gains cannot be isolated from classroom instruction
About 50% attrition limits generalization to persisters only
Modest effect sizes overall
target_learners: Adults with basic reading skills below the seventh grade level
target_learning_goals: Decoding accuracy and efficiency
Word recognition
Reading fluency
examples: 148 completers received up to 45 one-on-one tutoring sessions of 75 minutes each across three programs adapted from child-focused interventions
key_sources: Sabatini John P., Shore Jane, Holtzman Steven, Scarborough Hollis S. (2011). Relative Effectiveness of Reading Intervention Programs for Adults with Low Literacy. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3269067/

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Sublation (Aufhebung) as a framework for integrating guidance and discovery in the discovery learning debate
description: The article proposes Hegel's concept of sublation (Aufhebung) as a way to end the one-dimensional tug of war between minimal guidance and direct instruction. Aufheben has three senses: to lift up to a higher level, to preserve elements of both sides of a tension in a new integration, and to abolish the tension. The author argues the debate should integrate "justified concerns from both opposite positions" rather than pick a winner.
requirements: The debate must move beyond dichotomized comparisons of discovery versus instruction extremes for sublation to operate.
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal for the field, not an empirically tested intervention.
target_learners: All learners in instructional settings where discovery and guidance are balanced
target_learning_goals: Understanding what cannot be told but must be discovered or reinvented
examples: The author reads Trninic's martial arts case study as dissolving the dichotomies, since repetition and continued guidance coexist with student discovery.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Support collaborative inquiry learning with communication instruction plus inquiry prompts to raise team regulation and improve performance
description: The article concludes that collaborative inquiry environments should provide both communication instruction and inquiry-support tools, because "different measures of support can enhance the use of team regulative activities, which in turn can lead to better learning results". Communication instruction (RIDE) raised team regulation, but only the condition that added the CHT's inquiry prompts showed team regulation relating positively to learning results. The authors also recommend building in mirroring or metacognitive tools so students learn how and when to regulate.
requirements: Support must target both the collaboration process (communication instruction) and the inquiry process (prompting tools)
constraints: The study could not attribute the learning-result relation to the CHT alone versus the combination of supports; the 90-minute session limits robust learning-outcome effects
target_learners: secondary school students in collaborative inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: regulation of collaborative learning processes and improved inquiry learning performance
examples: Dyads in the CHT condition received RIDE instruction plus the Collaborative Hypothesis Tool and showed a significant positive team-regulation–learning-result correlation
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3
title: Integrate instructional support into peer-feedback scenarios, prioritizing the feedback provision phase
description: Based on the meta-analytic findings, the authors recommend that practitioners integrate instructional support into peer-feedback processes, with the strongest and most consistent evidence for support presented during the feedback provision phase. They state that "increasing its effectiveness by almost one half of a standard deviation through the integration of instructional support is definitely notable and strongly suggests that it is worthwhile for practitioners to ponder about including further instructional support in the peer-feedback process". Generic provision support is the only type that also improved subject-matter-related knowledge.
requirements: A peer-feedback activity in which learners exchange task-related feedback on each other's task solutions, with a condition receiving the support and a comparable condition not receiving it
constraints: Evidence for supporting the feedback reception phase is too limited to interpret; effects on subject-matter-related knowledge were significant only for generic provision support
target_learning_goals: Quality of peer-feedback messages
Use of received feedback in revisions
Subject-matter-related knowledge
examples: Across the 32 included studies, support during feedback provision (e.g. rubrics, sentence starters, guiding questions, preparatory activities) was compared against unsupported peer-feedback, yielding g = 0.51 overall for provision support.
key_sources: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3

article_title: A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking
citation: Dave Neale & Deborah Pino-Pasternak. (2016). A Review of Reminiscing in Early Childhood Settings and Links to Sustained Shared Thinking. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9376-0
title: Sustained shared thinking: an episode-level construct for adult–child dialog in early childhood
description: Sustained shared thinking is a construct developed in the EPPE and REPEY studies, defined by Sylva et al. (2004) as an episode in which two or more individuals "work together" in an intellectual way to solve a problem, clarify a concept, evaluate activities, or extend a narrative, with both parties contributing and thinking developing and extending. The review characterizes it as exemplifying the field's focus on explicit learning situations and macro-level episode identification, contrasting it with the utterance-by-utterance elaborative style approach. It reports the construct as developmentally significant in large-scale research.
requirements: Identification of valid episodes of joint intellectual activity between adult and child
constraints: The review argues its identification involves a proscriptive focus on explicit learning tasks and lacks close utterance-by-utterance structural analysis, limiting usefulness in some ways
target_learners: Preschool children in formal early childhood settings
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and problem solving
Emergent literacy
Extension of narrative
examples: The review compares sustained shared thinking criteria with elaborative style analysis to draw out synergies and differences in classification and analysis

The supernormal divide into two groups: the specifically supernormal, in whom one mental phase (musical, artistic, mathematical, technical, linguistic) is strongly developed while others may be merely normal, and the universally supernormal, whose general superiority appears across diverse mental activity. The pedagogy of the supernormal must cover all forms and apply different programs to different phases.

constraints: A satisfactory psychological definition is impossible just now because scientific psychology is only beginning to study the problem; true geniuses are too rare for a special pedagogy

citation: Peney, T., & Skarratt, P. A. (2024). Increasing the immersivity of 360° videos facilitates learning and memory: implications for theory and practice. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10402-9
title: Surprise cued-recall test of incidental learning from a 360° video
description: An incidental learning assessment comprising 20 questions about a three-minute 360° film, administered as a surprise after viewing. Fifteen questions targeted events at specific timepoints and five were foils concerning events that did not occur, with negative responses coded as correct. Questions were presented in a unique random order for each participant on the same device on which they viewed the film. citation: Jere-Folotiya, J., Chansa-Kabali, T., Munachaka, J. C., Sampa, F., Yalukanda, C., Westerholm, J., Richardson, U., Serpell, R., & Lyytinen, H. (2014). description: The article recommends using GraphoGame as a supplement to regular literacy teaching and targeting both learners and their teachers. "It further suggests that intervention with the game should focus on both students and teachers, as the greatest effect was observed when the students and teachers were both exposed to the game." Teacher exposure is meant to align classroom instruction with the game's phonics approach and avoid interference from English letter names.

article_title: Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory
citation: Hauert, S., Luo, T., & Yen, C.-J. (2026). Assessing the impact of substituting interaction types: an empirical study of the interaction equivalency theory. Education Tech Research Dev, 74, 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10563-1
title: Substitute learner–content interaction for learner–learner interaction when interpersonal interaction is not required by the instructional objective
description: Based on the trial's findings, the article recommends that designers first determine whether a learning experience requires interpersonal interaction for an instructional objective or ancillary purpose such as community building. If not, learner–content interactions "impose a lower perceived workload and a higher perceived level of learning" while correlating to higher measured performance, and can be substituted for learner–learner interactions without impacting performance. This relieves instructors of moderation workload and frees capacity for interpersonal interactions where they matter.
requirements: Front-end analysis must first determine whether interpersonal interaction is needed to accomplish an instructional objective or ancillary purpose such as building a sense of community or collaboration
constraints: Evidence comes from adult learners in one undergraduate, law-related occupational program with explicit, declarative content over one week; results may not generalize to other populations, knowledge types, or contexts
target_learners: adult distance-education students in formal online undergraduate programs
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition of explicit, declarative content without degrading measured performance
examples: In the study, designers should also evaluate which tools and methods best operationalize each interaction type; the authors note interactive multimedia with real-time feedback can enhance timely assessment while creating instructor capacity

citation: Czerniewicz, L. & Brown, C. (2009). A study of the relationship between institutional policy, organisational culture and elearning use in four South African universities. Computers & Education, 53, 121-131. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2009.01.006
title: Institutional elearning policies should be supportive, flexible and non-restrictive so as to frame staff innovation while sustaining a culture that fosters varied pedagogical practices
description: The article concludes that policies are needed but must enable rather than compel: "supportive, flexible, non-restrictive institutional policies would be the most useful frames for staff innovation in the classroom". It argues successful, embedded and innovative ICT-teaching practices are likely the product of both enabling institutional policies and conducive collegium or enterprise cultures, suggesting a Structured Collegium or Structured Enterprise type as closest to the needed coalescence.
requirements: Policy understood as allocation of goals, values and resources, including centralised support structures and institution-wide systems
constraints: The article warns top-down corporate approaches may not be consultative enough and may be resented or resisted, with staff perceiving ICTs as forced
Neither the Structured Collegium nor Structured Enterprise type was found among the four institutions studied, so the recommendation is extrapolated
target_learning_goals: effective and innovative elearning use in teaching and learning
examples: The study found Structured Corporate types achieved critical mass while the Unstructured Collegium fostered staff variety of use, motivating the call for policies that support and enable while sustaining innovation
