article_title: Experiences of using a public key infrastructure for the preparation of examination papers
citation: David W Chadwick, Rana Tassabehji and Andrew Young. (1999). Experiences of Using a Public Key Infrastructure for the Preparation of Examination Papers. IT Institute, University of Salford. http://www.salford.ac.uk/its024/X500.htm
title: Three user types — Supporter, Potential Supporter and Resister — profile how staff adopt an electronic process
description: From questionnaire and interview profiling of pilot participants, the authors derive "a profile of 3 types of user". The Supporter is enthusiastic, needs no post-implementation support and actively counters problems; the Potential Supporter is enthusiastic but needs practice, training, documentation and an assisting infrastructure; the Resister prefers established paper processes, sees new processes as extra burden, and treats technical hiccups as an excuse to delay or abandon the system. Each type is characterised by course tenure, age, attitudes and thoughts scores, home Internet access and security-software knowledge.
requirements: A full assessment of the types and profiles of users in the organisation before change is attempted, so implementation can be tailored to their differing needs
constraints: Derived from an admittedly small sample of computer-literate departments; the authors state further study is needed for less computer-frequent departments
target_learners: university lecturers and administrators adopting new electronic processes
target_learning_goals: understanding and adopting a new secure electronic work process
examples: Profiling distinguished ITI lecturers (technology oriented, mostly supporters) from CMS staff, where one respondent with markedly low thoughts-about-computers scores predicted resistance that materialised mid-pilot

citation: Mehrvarz, Mahboobe; Heidari, Elham; Farrokhnia, Mohammadreza; Noroozi, Omid. (2021). The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance. Computers & Education 167 (2021) 104184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104184
title: Support both students' digital competence and their out-of-class digital informal learning to enhance academic performance
description: Because the study found digital competence directly improves academic performance and DIL carries an additional indirect effect, the authors recommend dual support. They state that higher education institutions, educators and curriculum designers "should not only improve the students' digital competence through extra-curricular programs", but also "should provide opportunities for students to learn outside the formal classes through digital environments". The recommendation rests on the confirmed partial-mediation model, and the authors also urge university policy-makers to attend to informal learning contexts alongside formal learning.
requirements: Institutions must offer both competence-building programs and digital environments usable outside formal classes
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional SEM without any empirical intervention, so the recommendation is not validated experimentally
target_learning_goals: academic performance
digital competence
examples: The authors suggest future research focus on specific strategies for developing students' digital competence and DIL and on strategies that can make students use DIL

title: Provide supports for change at pedagogical design, administrative, resource and professional-development levels
description: The article states that teachers who make the most changes in the classroom are those with the greatest level of support, and that supports need to be at the levels of "pedagogical design, coordinator support, administrative support" and "the provision of the required resources and appropriate continuing professional development". The UNITE project sought to create this support structure to ensure maximal benefits of the e-/m-Learning system for teaching and learning.
requirements: Supports must span pedagogical design, coordinator and administrative support, resources, and continuing professional development
constraints: Support needs are greatest where teacher change is expected

examples: The project put supports for change in place at the levels of pedagogical design, administrative support and the provision of the required resources and appropriate continuing professional development.

article_title: Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Quinn, D. M., Lynch, K., & Kim, J. S. (2014). Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-analysis. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Summer counterfactual account: income moderation flipped after 1998 because the higher-income summer counterfactual changed
description: An explanatory framework the authors propose for why Cooper et al.'s (2000) review found higher-income students benefited more from summer school while their 1998–2011 reviews find the opposite. They hypothesize that rising returns to family income reflect increased parental investment in cognitive development, so "the summer counterfactual for the average higher income student may have changed" between review periods. Because treatment/control contrasts depend on nonparticipants' summer loss or gain, the higher-income contrast may be weaker today. The article also acknowledges chance, given small numbers of studies, as an alternative explanation.
requirements: Requires comparison of summer treatment/control contrasts across historical periods with differing out-of-school counterfactuals for higher-income students
constraints: Offered as "one hypothesis"; the authors note the discrepancy could be "due simply to chance, particularly when sample sizes... are small"
target_learners: Kindergarten to Grade 8 students in the United States and Canada
target_learning_goals: Math and reading achievement over the summer vacation months
examples: The authors contrast Cooper et al.'s 1966–1998 review window with their 1998–2011 window and note migrant workers' children showed some of the largest effect sizes in Cooper et al.'s review

article_title: The Impact of Stratified Teaching on the Academic Performance of Chinese Middle School Students: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Shi, H., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, A.C.K. (2020) The impact of stratified teaching on the academic performance of Chinese middle school students: A meta-analysis. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 7(1):735-760. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.20.re012
title: Provide sustained psychological care and encouragement across all levels during stratified teaching to prevent labeling burden
description: The article reports that under any stratification mode, students "are often labeled with A, B, and C levels, which creates psychological problems for middle and low-level students with some kinds of hint". Teachers typically counsel students early in stratification, but later inattention can cause psychological imbalance, especially at the extremes. The principle requires care and encouragement throughout the whole implementation period, not only at the start.
requirements: Teachers must communicate and psychologically counsel students at different levels early in stratification and continue attention throughout implementation.
constraints: The article states the problem arises across recessive, dominant, and shift-class stratification alike.
target_learning_goals: academic performance
student well-being and motivation
examples: The article notes that lack of later-stage attention can easily cause students' psychological imbalance, especially those at the extremes.

article_title: Surgical Sabermetrics: A Scoping Review of Technology-enhanced Assessment of Nontechnical Skills in the Operating Room.
citation: Howie Emma E., Ambler Olivia, Gunn Eilidh G.M., Dias Roger D., Wigmore Stephen J., Skipworth Richard J.E., Yule Steven J. (2024). title: Surgical sabermetrics: digital, sensor-based assessment of operative nontechnical skills organized by the NOTSS taxonomy with cognitive load as an added construct
description: Surgical sabermetrics is the practice of digital assessment for feedback and improvement in surgery, influenced by performance monitoring in elite sports. It integrates audio-visual capture of the operating room with sensor-based assessment of the surgeon and team, and clinical data. The review organizes the field by the NOTSS taxonomy (Situation Awareness, Decision-Making, Communication, Teamwork, Leadership) and introduces cognitive load as an additional nontechnical construct, defining nontechnical skills as "cognitive, social and personal resource skills that complement technical skills and contribute to safe and efficient task performance."
requirements: Studies must digitally measure at least one nontechnical skill per the NOTSS taxonomy, including CogL, in a surgical context
constraints: Objective metrics are proxy measures of performance variables of interest; interpretation of the surgical context is required to derive meaning, and ground truth is required to determine the validity

cognitive load management
surgical performance improvement
examples: The review mapped 122 distinct objective digital metrics across 16 categories against NOTSS domains in Supplemental Table 2, with cardiovascular measures such as HRV the most frequently used (n=25 studies).

citation: Ngo Hazel, Sokolovic Nina, Hu Julia, Jenkins Jennifer. (2025). A systematic review identifying effective teaching methods and their combinations for increasing empathy in physicians: pairwise and network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07917-x
title: Effective empathy interventions combine at least one surface-learning and one deep-learning teaching method
description: Across the SUCRA rankings, the article observes that significant teaching-method combinations pair a content-mastery component with an experiential component: "the combinations of teaching methods that show statistically significant effect sizes (see Fig. 3) include at least one 'surface learning' component (mastery of content) and at least one 'deep learning' component (connections between, and extension of, the content)". Didactic supplies the cognitive framework, while rehearsal or reflection provides application and consolidation. The article reports the didactic-plus-experiential (rehearsal and reflection) combinations were the most effective.
requirements: At least one didactic (surface) component paired with an experiential component such as rehearsal or reflection
constraints: Top-ranked two-method combinations had wide confidence intervals due to few contributing studies
target_learning_goals: empathy skills
examples: The NMA's top-ranked combinations DH and DR each pair didactic with one experiential method

article_title: A systematic review of the effects of residency training on patient outcomes.
citation: van der Leeuw Renée M, Lombarts Kiki MJMH, Arah Onyebuchi A, Heineman Maas Jan. (2012). A systematic review of the effects of residency training on patient outcomes. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3391170/

developing operative competence through supervised exposure

article_title: Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review.
citation: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). title: Continue simulation programs over time rather than treating them as one-time interventions, since teamwork gains decay without ongoing training
description: The review's evidence indicates that simulation-based CRM training effects on workplace behaviour are not automatically durable: in the interrupted time series study, "All CTS measures returned to baseline during the decay phase" once the in situ simulation program stopped, and in another study transfer of CRM skills in the workplace was not retained after a month. constraints: All of the studies included in this review involved one time-limited intervention on a small number of subjects; the authors note it is possible that modification of patient outcome requires a whole series of interventions on many subjects
target_learners: Multidisciplinary trauma and emergency teams, including physicians, residents, nurses, technicians, pharmacists, and respiratory therapists
target_learning_goals: Sustained transfer of teamwork and communication behaviours to real clinical settings
examples: The interrupted time series study compared teamwork behaviours over four periods — pre-test baseline, didactic-based phase, simulation phase, and decay phase — and found all CTS measures returned to baseline during the decay phase

article_title: Increasing Pre-Kindergarten Early Literacy Skills in Children with Developmental Disabilities and Delays
citation: Pears, K. C., Kim, H. K., Fisher, P., & Yoerger, K. (2016). Increasing pre-kindergarten early literacy skills in children with developmental disabilities and delays. Journal of School Psychology, 57, 15-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2016.05.004

description: The article argues that the transition into school is an optimal time to intervene on school readiness, and that academic-year calendars create "a summer services gap during which the most vulnerable, highest-risk children may lose or fail to gain valuable skills". A short-term intensive summer program delivered just before kindergarten entry, followed by maintenance sessions in the first months of kindergarten, can augment early intervention services and boost literacy and self-regulation before school starts. constraints: The authors caution this is not a single solution; children are likely to require a number of services across time, and many children remained at risk after the intervention

target_learning_goals: School readiness, especially early literacy skills, prior to kindergarten entry
examples: KITS delivered 16 child sessions in the two months before kindergarten and 8 sessions in the first two months of kindergarten, with parent groups running in parallel

citation: Muhammad Ali Mustapha. (2018). Use of Suggestopedia to Improve Students’ Listening Skill in English Language. i-manager’s Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 4. https://www.i-manager.com/journals/journal_of_english_language_teaching
title: Suggestopedia: Lozanov's suggestion-based humanistic language-teaching method
description: Suggestopedia is a language-teaching method introduced by Georgi Lozanov in the 1970s that applies the power of "suggestion" to pedagogy to help learners eliminate negative feelings, making students feel relaxed during teaching and learning. The article describes it as a humanistic method that uses aesthetic galleries, musical sounds and suggestions to remove anxiety, emotion and fear that might preoccupy learners, on the premise that when anxiety and bad impressions are removed students learn easier and faster. It is often claimed to teach languages approximately three times as quickly as conventional methods.
requirements: A classroom environment using aesthetic gadgets, musical sounds and suggestion so that learner anxiety and negative feelings are removed
constraints: Originally applied mainly in foreign language teaching; the speed claim is reported as an often-made claim, not a finding of this study
target_learners: senior secondary school students (SS II, aged 16-17) learning English as a second/foreign language
target_learning_goals: English listening skill
second-language proficiency (also reported for reading and speaking)
examples: The experimental group was taught the topic 'The Journey through Pathholed Road' using suggestopedia while the control group studied the same topic with conventional methods over eight weeks

description: The article argues that vocabulary items need repeated meaningful exposure to be acquired, citing the recommendation that "six to ten meaningful encounters with a vocabulary item is the minimum necessary for the item to have a potential to be acquired". Because most target words in this study were used only in the classroom context, their learnability was diminished, and the authors commit to ensuring sufficient exposure in future studies.

constraints: Rare and off-list words used only in classroom context may decline on delayed posttests and may compromise student motivation

article_title: The Effect of Length of Exposure to CALL Technology on Young Iranian EFL Learners' Grammar Gain
citation: Karim Sadeghi & Masoumeh Dousti. (2013). The Effect of Length of Exposure to CALL Technology on Young Iranian EFL Learners' Grammar Gain. English Language Teaching, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n2p14
title: Allocate sufficient exposure time to CALL activities, since longer exposure sustained grammar gains over time
description: The article concludes that the amount of time devoted to CALL matters for young learners' grammar learning: the group with double the exposure time was the only one to retain a significant advantage on the delayed post-test. The authors state that "the increase in the time allocation will lead to the increase in learners' grammar gain" and suggest the findings indicate the appropriate amount of time needed in young learners' classes. Teachers and administrators are advised to review curricula and consider incorporating CALL with adequate time allocation.
requirements: CALL activities must be integrated into scheduled class time with sufficient session length
Technology must be available in the teaching environment
constraints: The advantage of longer exposure appeared only on the delayed post-test, not the immediate one
Findings come from one small quasi-experiment with 45 young beginner learners in Iran
target_learning_goals: grammar gain and retention
examples: The second experimental group used the software for half an hour per session versus a quarter hour for the first group, and alone retained a significant advantage two weeks later

title: Supplemental blended learning model combining face-to-face teaching with asynchronous app-based practice
description: The study implements the supplemental model from Twigg's (2003) course-design typology, in which a small online supplement is added to a traditional face-to-face course. The control group received face-to-face teaching with six in-class hours per week, while the experimental group combined the same classroom teaching with asynchronous Memrise use outside scheduled class time. The article situates this on a spectrum of blended definitions ranging from a small online supplement to fully online delivery.
requirements: Online content should run parallel with the content being taught in the classroom
constraints: The article states there are "no certain rules to define what the ideal blend might be"; the emphasis is on developing an optimal blend exploiting the best of available modes
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge in English
examples: The experimental group studied about 260 words of the first 400 TOEFL items over a 4-week instruction period before taking the post-test

article_title: The Effect of Project-Based History and Nature of Science Practices on the Change of Nature of Scientific Knowledge
citation: Ayşe Sert Çıbık. (2016). The Effect of Project-Based History and Nature of Science Practices on the Change of Nature of Scientific Knowledge. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 453-472.
title: SUSSI questionnaire (Student Understanding of Science and Scientific Inquiry)
description: SUSSI is a dual-response instrument mixing quantitative and qualitative approaches: it "combines Likert -scale items and related open-ended questions" to determine views on nature of scientific knowledge development across six elements, with four Likert items per part plus one open-ended question, 24 Likert items and six open-ended questions in total. In this study it was translated into Turkish, validated through translation, expert review and pilot testing, and administered as pre-test and post-test to both groups.
requirements: Translation, expert construct-validity checks and pilot testing were carried out before use with Turkish pre-service teachers
constraints: The article notes quantitative NOS instruments alone leave a gap between researchers' interpretations and students' actual answers, and qualitative instruments are time-consuming with large groups
target_learning_goals: views of the nature of scientific knowledge across six aspects including observations and inferences, tentativeness, theories and laws, social and cultural embeddedness, creativity, and scientific methods
examples: Administered as pre-test and post-test to experimental (N:41) and control (N:46) groups; overall Cronbach Alpha was 0.67, with aspect values from 0.62 to 0.68

article_title: The Impact of a Junior High School Community Intervention Project: Moving beyond the Testing Juggernaut and into a Community of Creative Learners
citation: Nelson, L. P., McMahan, S. K., & Torres, T. (2012). The Impact of a Junior High School Community Intervention Project: Moving Beyond the Testing Juggernaut and Into a Community of Creative Learners. School Community Journal, 22(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ970682
title: Build sustainable, collaborative, community-based mentoring programs that develop student creativity rather than pursuing test scores alone
description: The authors make "an argument for sustainable, collaborative, and organic community-based mentoring programs" focused on developing students' creativity as a means to improve school practices. The principle holds that connecting students with committed adult role models from the community improves attendance, morale, and perceptions of school, but only when school leadership cooperates and programs are sustained beyond initial funding. It arises directly from a case where year-one gains reversed once leadership prioritized testing exclusively.
requirements: A committed group of community leaders such as businesses, nonprofits, education partners, faith-based organizations, parents, and civic organizations
Adequate funding so that new community partnerships that are working stay focused and on task
Cooperation of school leadership to sustain the programs
constraints: Efforts to sustain positive school climate changes without the cooperation of school leadership were entirely ineffective in this study
target_learners: Junior high school students in high-risk urban schools
target_learning_goals: Student engagement, attendance, and perceptions of school climate
Development of student creativity
examples: The afterschool soccer club, which required class attendance and acceptable grades and was coached by university physical education teacher education candidates, was the only program sustained beyond the project, later funded for five more years and expanded into seven other junior high schools

article_title: Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities
citation: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514.
title: Embedding eight research skills into regular subject lessons through subject-specific task lists
description: The article maps each of eight research skills onto concrete tasks in regular elementary subjects: mathematics, native language, literary reading, environment and technology. For example, the ability to see the problem is practiced in mathematics by finding text with excessive or insufficient content, in native language by composing a story as solving a problem, and in environment by observing natural phenomena. The ability to structure materials is practiced by making plans of text and representing data in tables and diagrams. This pattern operationalizes research-skill formation inside existing subject teaching rather than in a separate course.
requirements: Tasks must be selected so that each subject's ordinary content exercises a named research skill such as hypothesizing, questioning, classifying or proving
constraints: The task lists are illustrative content specifications for elementary-school subjects in the Russian curriculum context
target_learners: junior pupils aged 7-11 in elementary school
target_learning_goals: seeing problems, proposing hypotheses, asking questions, classifying, structuring materials, making discourse, proving ideas, representing results
examples: Technology tasks for representing results include making visual aids from paper and plasticine, composing digital publications with clickable links, and preparing presentations.

citation: Yucetoker, I. (2016). The visual memory-based memorization techniques in piano education. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 65, 111-128. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.65.07
title: Support visual learners' memorization with color and shape-based visual elements
description: For students with strong visual memory, piano teachers should use colored pens, shapes, and visual groupings on sheet music to mark themes, harmonic functions, and formal elements. This supports memorization by making structural features visually salient and reducing the difficulty of locating themes in complex contrapuntal works.
requirements: Identify students with strong visual learning style before applying
constraints: Tested only with visual students; other learner types need separate approaches

examples: 6-week intervention using color-coded note cards with Bach inventions

article_title: Supported Self-Explaining during Fraction Intervention
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Malone, A., Schumacher, R. F., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2015). Supported Self-Explaining during Fraction Intervention. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Supported self-explaining: learners operate on high-quality explanations already created for them, grounded in the generative model of learning
description: The article distinguishes three forms of self-explaining: spontaneous, elicited, and "supported self-explaining, in which learners operate on high-quality explanations already created for them." Because at-risk learners may invent subpar explanations, tutors modeled high-quality explanations and gave practice analyzing and applying them, encouraging elaboration and discussion. The approach rests on the generative model of learning (Wittrock, 1990), which posits that "learning requires actively processing and elaborating on the to-be-learned information while meaningfully connecting new information to existing knowledge," and is hypothesized to work by decreasing cognitive load.
requirements: Learners must receive modeled high-quality explanations and practice analyzing and applying them, with encouragement to elaborate on and discuss important features of the explanations.
constraints: The article identifies no previous randomized control trial testing this form of supported explaining among at-risk students prior to this study.
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude comparison
conceptual explanation of why fractions differ in magnitude
examples: Tutors modeled a 4-step sequence in which students labeled problem type, evaluated a good drawing, labeled drawings with numerical values, and wrote a sentence explaining why the circled fraction was greater.

article_title: Research on Group Learning and Cognitive Science: A Study of Motivation, Knowledge, and Self-Regulation in a Large Lecture College Algebra Class
citation: David Miller and Matthew Schraeder. (2015). Research on Group Learning and Cognitive Science: A Study of Motivation, Knowledge, and Self-Regulation in a Large Lecture College Algebra Class. The Mathematics Educator, Vol. 24, No. 2, 27-55. https://tme.coe.uga.edu/
title: Supplemental Practice day with group worked-example worksheets in a large lecture course
description: A weekly extra class day added to a two-lecture-plus-lab large course structure, in which students form ad hoc groups and complete worksheets presenting an expert's solution followed by a similar problem to work out. Each worksheet contained "approximately 8 to 10 worked examples and problems," reviewing the previous week's lecture content with no new material, while two to three undergraduate assistants and a graduate student circulated to answer questions. The design was modeled after worked-example research and implemented in 13 SP days per semester.

class assistants ready to help students during SP days
worksheets presenting a worked solution followed by a problem for students to work
constraints: Due to time constraints, not all topics from the previous week's lecture were covered on the worksheets
it was not plausible to prevent students from referencing the worked example while completing the paired problem, unlike prior laboratory studies
problems varied in similarity to the worked examples
target_learners: college students in large lecture introductory mathematics courses, including freshmen and sophomores
target_learning_goals: college algebra problem solving
course success rates
prior knowledge growth
examples: Worksheets 3 and 11 in the 5th and 13th SP sessions presented worked examples in two-column format with textbook section references students could consult outside class

title: Supervise preschool computer use and restrict it to formal education purposes within the teaching-learning process
description: The article sets conditions for implementing computer-assisted education in preschool: adult oversight and educational purpose. It states that "supervision by parents or teachers should be done, the computer should be used in teaching-learning process, the computer should not be used for social media or game purposes". The principle operationalizes computer use as a supervised instructional instrument rather than an entertainment device.
requirements: Supervision by parents or teachers during children's computer use
The computer is used within the teaching-learning process for formal education purposes
constraints: The computer should not be used for social media or game purposes

title: Support preschool teachers with seminars, courses, and supportive science training so they can use computers actively
description: Because the study found computer-assisted education beneficial and found teachers avoiding science activities, the article recommends professional development. It states that "the preschool teachers should be supported by giving them seminars and courses to use computers in their classes actively", and that teachers who feel inadequate in science "should be given supportive science training and their knowledge levels should be increased".

Supportive science training that raises teachers' knowledge levels in science subjects

title: Set of more than 60 supplementary writing exercises for well-organized writing
description: In the experimental group, the same textbooks as the control group were used, but "about more than 60 supplementary exercises was used in order to develop the skills in the field of well-organized writing." The exercises include grouping food words into categories, completing the skeleton of an outline from a passage about insects, and writing a paragraph on a chosen topic followed by partner discussion. article_title: Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga
citation: Sunardi, Herman J. Waluyo, Astini Suudi, Nugraheni Eko Wardani. (2018). Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://www.mojet.net
title: Suggestopedia: music-supported suggestive teaching that removes psychological hindrances to learning
description: Suggestopedia is a strategy developed by Lozanov, applied in this study through background music with suggestive lyrics. The article states that "the main factor that hindered the students’ learning, including learning language and literature, is the psychological hindrance," and that the hindrance "can be eliminated by incorporating drama, physical activities, and music in the lesson." Relaxation and concentration techniques are held to open students' subconscious and help them master new vocabulary and structures. In this study the approach was realised through tembang dolanan rhymes with inserted suggestive sentences.
requirements: A fun, relaxing teaching atmosphere is described as "a prerequisite of this strategy"; Scovel's techniques include comfortable seating, background music, dim light, increased individual participation, posters, and teachers trained in suggestive teaching arts.
constraints: The article locates the approach in primary language and literature lessons in Salatiga; effectiveness evidence comes from this study's trials only.
target_learners: Primary school students (fifth grade) learning Bahasa Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Storytelling skill in Bahasa Indonesia, including vocabulary, pronunciation, expression, and confident oral performance
examples: Tembang dolanan (Javanese nursery rhymes) with inserted suggestive sentences were used to produce relaxing, motivating and entertaining effects during storytelling lessons.
key_sources: Sunardi, Herman J. Waluyo, Astini Suudi, Nugraheni Eko Wardani. (2018). Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165473

article_title: Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga
citation: Sunardi, Herman J. Waluyo, Astini Suudi, Nugraheni Eko Wardani. (2018). Suggestopedia Based Storytelling Teaching Model for Primary Students in Salatiga. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 6, Issue 1. https://www.mojet.net
title: Suggestopedia-based storytelling teaching model: a four-stage procedural development pattern
description: The article develops a procedural teaching model — a systematic procedure to organize learning experiences to meet learning objectives — through four stages adapted from Borg and Gall: "1) preliminary research and needs analysis, 2) design and development of the model prototype, 3) limited and general trial, and 4) effectiveness test." The model combines suggestopedia with group work, socio-drama play, discussion to compose stories, and performance, with the teacher acting as facilitator rather than the center of the lesson.
requirements: Teaching scenarios must be executed by teachers according to the prescribed procedures; the model should be equipped with an assessment rubric to grade students' performance.
constraints: The model was developed and tested with fifth graders in Salatiga primary schools; the article states the prototype "can be further developed to increase the primary students’ story telling skill in Salatiga."

target_learning_goals: Bahasa Indonesia storytelling skill, active and creative participation, teamwork, and self-confidence

article_title: E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization
citation: Yachina, N. P., Valeeva, L. A., & Sirazeeva, A. F. (2016). E-Teaching Materials as the Means to Improve Humanities Teaching Proficiency in the Context of Education Informatization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-442.
title: Model of subject-oriented training of future humanities teachers based on e-teaching materials
description: The article presents a model of subject-oriented training of future humanities teachers built on e-teaching materials, exemplified in the 'Teaching proficiency' course. citation: Altintas, E., & Ozdemir, A. S. (2015). Evaluating a Newly Developed Differentiation Approach in Terms of Student Achievement and Teachers' Opinions. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2540
title: A subject-based differentiation approach for teaching mathematics to gifted students built on project-based learning, multiple intelligences, and enrichment.
description: The article develops a differentiation approach for teaching mathematics to gifted middle-school students that modifies content, process, product, and learning environment relative to the national curriculum. Content is defined as "enriched objectives + theme", process incorporates "determining the students' multiple intelligence domains + teachers' strategies + basic skills + research skills + productive skills", and the learning environment combines "creative thinking + multiple-intelligences + different disciplines + project-based". The approach draws on the Williams, Maker, Kaplan, and autonomous learner models and Gardner's multiple intelligences, with particular emphasis on Maker matrix Type III and Type V problems. Students select project topics aligned with their dominant intelligence domains and complete all project stages including problem definition, method, and presentation.

Teachers must be informed about creativity, project preparation steps, and project evaluation processes before implementation.
constraints: The approach was developed and evaluated specifically for mathematics instruction with gifted middle-school students in grades 5–7 in Turkish schools.

creative thinking and research skills

title: Supplantation-concreteness hypothesis for desktop VR efficacy, with channel noise and cognitive load as overriding negative influences
description: The article's theoretical framework combined supplantation theory, cognitive load theory, Dale's Cone of Experience for media concreteness, communication theory (channel noise), and Lowenfeld's visual/haptic perceptual typology within Cronbach and Snow's ATI research design model. The supplantation-concreteness hypothesis holds that VR's supplantation of mental imagery requirements and its experiential concreteness lead to better learning performance than still imagery. The article states that "the addition in the present study of channel overload noise and cognitive load in the form of a much more visually and navigationally complex VR environment encompassing two operating rooms appears to have caused override of the supplantation-concreteness benefits of VR, particularly for learners of the Low Visual percpetual type."
requirements: The framework requires consideration of learner perceptual type, task visual complexity, and the instructional treatment medium together.
constraints: Channel noise and cognitive overload from complex visual fields can override the supplantation-concreteness benefits of VR.
target_learners: Learners of visual and haptic perceptual types in technical training
target_learning_goals: Scenic orientation, recall of scenic details, and confidence in comprehending complex visual environments
examples: The study re-examined Ausburn and Ausburn's supplantation-concreteness hypothesis in a surgical technology training environment with two operating rooms.

citation: Waynick, J., Hussaini, S. S., Stonerook, E., Hiatt, T., Sisson, C., Peacock, B., O'Neal, S., McKinnond, A., Steele, L., & Gillette, C. (2026). Using academic admissions data to predict PA training attrition and academic difficulties: a survival analysis approach. Medical Education Online, 31(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2745370
title: Survival analysis as a framework for modeling attrition and academic difficulty as time-to-event processes rather than dichotomous outcomes.
description: The article advances a methodological framework that treats attrition and academic probation as time-to-event outcomes modeled with semi-parametric multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, rather than as dichotomous variables measured at a single point. The authors argue that "using dichotomous outcomes may obscure the complex, multifactorial nature of attrition, which unfolds over time" and that a time-to-event framework "allows risk to vary across the course of training." They apply this framework to a complete cohort of PA students using undergraduate admissions metrics as predictors, presenting results as adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The framework is guided by the academic integration component of Tinto's Student Integration Theory.
requirements: Requires longitudinal administrative data tracking students from matriculation through event or censoring, with time measured in intervals (here, weeks per academic unit with interval censoring).
constraints: The authors note only three prior studies had used time-to-event frameworks in health professions education, and that extrapolating findings across professions may be inappropriate because predictors do not operate independently of the educational environment.
target_learners: Physician associate (PA) students in graduate-entry professional programs
target_learning_goals: Identifying students at risk of academic probation and attrition to inform admissions decisions and early academic support
examples: The study applied Cox proportional hazards models to 605 PA student records from cohorts 2021–2027, modeling time to first probation and time to attrition with interval censoring at unit completion.

title: Taxonomy of surgical simulation technologies: VR, AR, MR, physical simulators, and computer-based simulations
description: The review organizes surgical simulation technologies into a typology, stating: "This section discusses four key types of simulation technologies: Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Physical Simulators, and Computer-Based Simulations." The review uses this taxonomy to map modalities to training purposes, noting low-fidelity task trainers suit early-stage learners while tissue and cadaver simulations offer the highest anatomical fidelity.
requirements: Modalities should be matched to training goals, e.g. VR for familiarization with anatomy and procedures and physical simulators for manual dexterity, as the review describes
constraints: The review notes fidelity, as defined by the Society for Simulation in Healthcare, includes physical, psychological, and environmental elements beyond technological accuracy
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skills
anatomical and procedural knowledge
decision-making under pressure
examples: The review describes VR laparoscopic and robotic simulations with feedback mechanisms, AR projection of anatomical models onto the patient, and task trainers for endoscopy or catheterization practice

target_learning_goals: Tolerance of clinical uncertainty
Adaptive clinical practice
Professional identity aligned with uncertainty
examples: Supervising physicians promoted epistemic distancing by guiding residents to identify knowledge gaps, which improved residents' sense of agency and adaptive practices

title: Universities should help nursing and midwifery undergraduates improve self-control and enhance self-efficacy during home-based e-learning
description: The article recommends that universities support students' self-regulation during home-based e-learning by strengthening self-control and self-efficacy. It states that "universities should assist nursing and midwifery undergraduates in improving self-control and enhancing self-efficacy to resist temptations and conquer difficulties when receiving HBEL". Suggested strategies include eliminating temptations before online classes, setting deadlines, planning ahead, and building self-efficacy through performance accomplishments, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and emotional arousal.
requirements: Interventions must target both self-control and self-efficacy, since the regression identified both as independent predictors of HBEL behavior.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and correlational, so the recommendation rests on associations rather than tested interventions in this study.

target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and quality of home-based e-learning behavior
examples: The article cites strategies such as blocking social media apps and muting phones before online classes, setting assignment deadlines, and assigning tasks from easy to difficult with positive feedback.

article_title: Investigating the association between variability in sulcal pattern and academic achievement.
citation: Roell M., Bellon E., Polspoel B., Declercq M. & De Smedt B. (2022). Investigating the association between variability in sulcal pattern and academic achievement. Scientific Reports 12, 12323. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-15335-y
title: Sulcal pattern as a developmental-constraint marker for studying biological origins of academic ability
description: The article uses sulcal patterns as a neuroanatomical marker for investigating early cerebral constraints on academic achievement. Sulcal morphology is "determined in utero" and "is stable during development", so unlike grey matter or white matter measures it is not affected by brain maturation or learning, allowing researchers to study causes of individual differences independent of learning history. The approach classifies the IPS as sectioned vs not sectioned, the OTS as interrupted vs continuous, and the ACC as single vs double parallel type, using established anatomical protocols.
requirements: Requires structural T1 MRI data amenable to sulcus segmentation and reliable manual labeling of IPS, OTS and ACC by trained raters (inter-rater agreement about 80.59% in this study).
constraints: The article notes effects of sulcal morphology on academic achievement, if present, may be too small for typical samples and may only be visible in heterogeneous samples or at certain developmental stages.
target_learners: typically developing grade 4 children (about 10 years old)
target_learning_goals: understanding biological constraints on individual differences in reading and mathematics achievement
examples: The study classified IPS, OTS and ACC sulcal patterns in 97 grade 4 children from structural MRI and tested their associations with arithmetic, symbolic number comparison and reading measures.

article_title: The user experience design of a novel microscope within SurgiSim, a virtual reality surgical simulator.
citation: de Lotbiniere-Bassett M, Volpato Batista A, Lai C, El Chemaly T, Dort J, Blevins N, Lui J. (2022). The user experience design of a novel microscope within SurgiSim, a virtual reality surgical simulator. Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-022-02727-8
title: SurgiSim VR surgical simulator with integrated virtual operating room microscope
description: SurgiSim is a VR platform, built on the original CardinalSim platform, for exploration and manipulation of patient-specific anatomy generated from clinical CT imaging, supporting Oculus Rift S, Quest, or Quest 2 headsets plus a 2D Monitor Mode. It renders high-fidelity stereoscopic graphics with haptic feedback, uses machine-learning auto-segmentation of anatomic structures, and supports virtual dissections comparable with intraoperative video. "To our knowledge, SurgiSim is the first VR simulator to include a virtual microscope." Its microscope is modeled on the ZEISS Kinevo 900 and is free-floating rather than boom-attached. The first released version (VI) uses anonymized clinical CT imaging from selected skull base cases.
requirements: VR headset (Oculus Rift S, Quest, or Quest 2) or 2D Monitor Mode; clinical DICOM CT imaging data; supported haptic hardware
constraints: Given that SurgiSim employs CT imaging data, the platform is most applicable to the rehearsal of bony anatomy dissection, with initial focus on temporal bone dissection
target_learners: surgical residents and trainees in otolaryngology and neurosurgery
target_learning_goals: temporal bone dissection
surgical microscope maneuvering
patient-specific procedural rehearsal
examples: The VR OR scene includes a surgical table, instrument tray, Mayo stand, ceiling-mounted surgical light, and television screen; anatomical renderings come from the Neurosurgical Atlas and Stanford NeuroTraIn photogrammetry models

article_title: Examining the causal relationships between interpersonal motivation, engagement, and academic performance among university students.
citation: Ito Takamichi, Umemoto Takatoyo. (2022). Examining the causal relationships between interpersonal motivation, engagement, and academic performance among university students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0274229
title: University educators should support students' identified regulation and intrinsic motivation for interpersonal relationships in collaborative learning
description: Based on the validated path model, the article recommends that educators encourage students to realize the value and importance of interacting with others through cooperative learning, and help students find fun and excitement in interacting with others. The article states: "First, university educators need to support identified regulation among other interpersonal motivations." Once students identify with the value of interpersonal relationships, engagement follows, and instructors should also create learning environments allowing students to focus attention and actively participate in collaborative learning.
requirements: Learning environments that include collaborative or pair-work activities through which students can experience and value interpersonal relationships
constraints: The study was conducted at a single university, which the authors state decreases generalizability; collaboration was through dialogue between pairs, and results need verification with other cooperative learning methods, group sizes, and task content
target_learning_goals: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in collaborative learning
deep and creative thinking through dialogue with classmates
examples: In the study's classes, students paired freely, alternated speaker and listener roles halfway through pair work, and wrote individual reports quoting and building on their partner's ideas
